title: The fool's three pains
hookLine: the blind turtle again, and the fool who suffers three ways

cards: Someone at work mentions, in general, that people have been cutting corners on expenses. They don't look at anyone in particular. They don't need to.
Somewhere in the room, a face goes hot. The hundred and twenty-ninth discourse is about the fool and the wise person, and it starts with exactly that moment.
A fool, the Buddha says, thinks badly, speaks badly and acts badly. And such a person doesn't have to wait for any afterlife to suffer. They suffer here, in three ways.

teach.b: First: the fool is sitting in company, and people start talking about the kind of harm he's done. He thinks: they're talking about me.
Second: he sees a wrongdoer caught and punished by the king's men, and thinks: that could be me.
Third, the image that stays: resting quietly on a chair or a bed, his past wrongs come over him, the text says, the way the shadows of great mountain peaks fall across the land in the evening.
The discourse then describes the lower realms after death in vivid, frightening detail.
And it returns to an image you met at the start of this year: the blind turtle.
A man throws a yoke with a single hole into the ocean, and winds push it every way. A blind turtle surfaces once every hundred years. How likely is it to put its neck through that hole?
That would happen sooner, the Buddha says, than the fool, once fallen low, regains a human life. Then the bright side, in mirror image.

The wise person thinks, speaks and acts well, and has three joys here and now: easy in company, untroubled at the sight of punishment, and at rest in the evening as good deeds fall over them like those same mountain shadows.
Look back at the week: space inside, the real marvel, eighty years in robes, the tamed elephant, sesame and gravel, the light that fades. And now the turtle, surfacing once more.

how: Buddhist teachers in several traditions cite the blind turtle to stress how precious a human birth is, and Tibetan teachings list 'precious human birth' as the first of four thoughts that turn the mind toward practice.

o: a beggar who has fallen on hard times
a fool: one who thinks, speaks and acts badly
a person who has never studied the texts

games.q: the fool's three pains: tap the pairs.

s: in MN 129 the fool's suffering only begins after death
the Buddha describes three pains here and now, before the afterlife is mentioned.
the wise person has three matching joys in this life
easy in company, untroubled at punishment, at rest as good deeds fall over them.
the turtle in the simile comes up once a year
it surfaces once every hundred years, which is why finding the yoke is so unlikely.

games.q: you're resting quietly at evening, after a day of harm done to others. what does MN 129 say comes over you?
o: your wrongs, like mountain shadows falling at evening.
games.why: the text's picture is the shadows of great peaks spreading over the land at dusk. for the wise person, the same image is good deeds.

practice: Picture the wide ocean, a small wooden yoke drifting on it, and remember that you're here: alive, human, with a mind that can listen and change.
In this teaching a human life is a rare chance, so let one breath be a thank you for it. If an old regret falls over you like a mountain shadow, just let it be seen, and come back to the breath.

wordCard.voice: Bala. The fool: fearing they're talked about, fearing they'll be caught, and old wrongs falling over them like mountain shadows at evening.

orig.note: Pali bala: fool, literally a child or an immature person. MN 129 sets it against pandita, the wise.

carryVoice: Your line: the turtle and the yoke. A human life is a rare chance. A week, done.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 129, Balapandita Sutta (fools and the wise)
Samyutta Nikaya 56.48, Chiggala Sutta (the yoke with a hole)
